candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on the Gospel of John
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.6 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's self-identification at the arrest — 'I am he' (egō eimi) followed by the arresting party going backward and falling to the ground — Cyril reads as the deliberate Johannine theophanic intrusion into the Passion narrative. The 'I AM' Cyril links to the divine self-disclosure (Ex 3:14 ego eimi ho ōn); the falling-back is the standard biblical reaction of the unholy when confronted with theophany (cf. Ezek 1:28, Rev 1:17). Cyril's theological point: even at the moment of voluntary self-surrender, Christ's divinity is manifested visibly. The arrest happens only because Christ permits it, not because the arresting party has the power to take Him.

candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on the Gospel of John
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.11 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's rebuke of Peter — 'The cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?' — Cyril takes as the deliberate Johannine inversion of the Synoptic Gethsemane prayer ('let this cup pass from me'). John omits the Gethsemane agony entirely; instead, Christ at the moment of arrest already speaks the conformed-will resolution: the cup will be drunk. The 'shall I not drink' (ou mē piō auto) is rhetorical question expecting affirmative answer: of course He will drink, because the Father has given it. Cyril reads this as confirming the perfect alignment of the Son's incarnate will with the Father's eternal will, even at the moment of greatest stress. This grounds Cyril's later argument for the integrity of Christ's human will (against Apollinarian denial).

candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on the Gospel of John
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XI.36 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'My kingdom is not of this world (ek tou kosmou toutou): if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence' Cyril takes as the dominical pin against any theocratic or revolutionary reading of Christ's mission. The kingdom's NOT-FROM-HENCE (ek — out of, sourced in) does not mean NOT-FOR-HERE: it means not deriving its character from this-world's power structures (force, military conquest, political dominance). The kingdom IS for the world, but it operates by different means (suffering love, persuasive truth, sacramental presence). Cyril's reading establishes the theological frame for the Tewahedo monastic tradition's withdrawal-from-political-power as the proper kingdom-ethic, while still affirming the kingdom's universal scope.

candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on the Gospel of John
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.38 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Pilate's question — 'What is truth?' (ti estin alētheia) — Cyril treats with characteristic theological tragedy. Truth Himself stands before Pilate (Christ is the truth per 14:6); Pilate fails to recognize what is right in front of him. Cyril notes the absence of any answer from Christ: the only proper response to a question that misses what is already self-evidently present is silence. Pilate's tragic moment becomes the prototype of every subsequent encounter with Christ where the questioner cannot or will not see what is before them. The Tewahedo Good Friday liturgy preserves this moment with particular weight; the question and the silence stand as the textual icon of unbelief.
